passages.title: Signal Lost
passages.text:
The hiking trip had been Dad's idea, and for the first hour, Kenji made sure everyone knew he hated it. He held his phone above his head at every switchback, hunting for a signal that never came.

“It's called disconnecting,” Dad said cheerfully.

“It's called being cut off from civilization,” Kenji muttered.

By noon they reached a ridge where the trail split. The wooden sign had rotted, its arrows pointing at nothing. Dad pulled out a paper map and frowned. A gray wall of clouds was rolling over the far peaks.

“Which way?” Kenji asked, and for the first time his voice carried no sarcasm.

Dad turned the map one way, then another. Kenji leaned in. Without thinking, he traced the contour lines with his finger, the way his science teacher had shown them during the unit on topography. “These lines are close together here,” he said. “That's a cliff. The left trail goes down gradually. That has to be the way back to the lot.”

Dad looked at him for a long moment. “When did you learn that?”

“Eighth grade,” Kenji said. “Apparently I was listening.”

They reached the car just as the first heavy drops began to fall. Inside, rain drummed on the roof, and Kenji's phone buzzed back to life with a dozen notifications. He glanced at the screen, then turned it face down on the seat.

“So,” he said, “where are we going next month?”

passages.title: Should Middle Schools Start Later?
passages.text:
Across the country, many middle schools begin classes before 8:00 a.m. Some districts have moved their start times later, arguing that students learn better when they are well-rested. Others say later start times create more problems than they solve.

Supporters of later start times point to biology. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. In districts that have shifted later, researchers have reported improvements in attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class.

Opponents raise practical concerns. Changing bell schedules can affect bus routes, since many districts use the same buses for elementary, middle, and high school students. Later dismissal times may cut into after-school sports, jobs, and family responsibilities such as caring for younger siblings. Some parents also worry that students will simply stay up later, erasing any benefit.

Some districts have found compromises. A few have reorganized bus routes so that younger students, who tend to wake up early, start first. Others have paired later start times with education programs that teach families about healthy sleep habits.

The debate shows that a seemingly simple question—what time should school start?—involves health, transportation, and family life. Any solution will require communities to weigh the evidence and the trade-offs carefully.

passages.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
passages.text:
In the port city of Verano, Master Ilse was known for maps so precise that sailors swore by them. When she agreed to take an apprentice, forty young people applied. She chose Tomas, a fisherman's son who could barely afford ink.

For months, Tomas did nothing but copy. He copied coastlines, rivers, and the curling script of place names until his wrist ached. He grew restless. Other apprentices in the city were already selling maps of their own.

“When will I make something new?” he finally asked.

Ilse set down her pen. “When you understand why each line is where it is.”

That spring, a captain came to the shop, furious. His ship had nearly run aground on a sandbar that wasn't on his map—a map Tomas recognized as one he had copied. Ilse examined it silently, then turned to Tomas. “You copied what was in front of you,” she said. “But the sea changes. Did you ask anyone where the sand had moved?”

Tomas's face burned. He had not.

The next morning, he borrowed his father's boat and spent a week sounding the harbor with a weighted rope, recording depths in a battered notebook. He talked to fishermen, who knew the shifting sandbars better than any chart.

When he returned, Ilse studied his notes for a long time. Then she slid a blank sheet of parchment across the table.

“Now,” she said, “make something new.”

passages.title: Learning from Failure: The Wright Brothers
passages.text:
On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright lay on the lower wing of a fragile aircraft near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The engine sputtered, the plane lifted off the sand, and for twelve seconds it flew. The flight covered only about 120 feet—shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet—but it changed the world.

That moment is often described as a sudden triumph. In reality, it was the result of years of failure. Beginning in 1899, Wilbur and Orville Wright built and tested a series of kites and gliders. Their 1901 glider performed so poorly that Wilbur reportedly said that humans would not fly in their lifetime.

Instead of quitting, the brothers questioned their data. They suspected that the published measurements they had relied on were wrong. To test their ideas, they built a small wind tunnel in their bicycle shop and tested more than 200 wing shapes. The results showed that the old data had overestimated the lift of curved wings.

Using their own measurements, the brothers designed a new glider in 1902. It flew hundreds of times. They also solved the problem of control by developing “wing warping,” a system that twisted the wings to help the pilot balance and turn.

The Wright brothers did not succeed because they never failed. They succeeded because they treated each failure as information. Their story suggests that persistence, combined with careful testing, can turn even discouraging setbacks into breakthroughs.

passages.title: From the Diary of a Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter, 1886
passages.text:
March 3 — Father's fever has not broken. The doctor from the mainland cannot cross until the gale passes, and Mother will not leave Father's side. That leaves the light to me.

I have watched Father tend the lamp a thousand times, but watching is not doing. Tonight I climbed the ninety-two steps with the oil can banging against my knees. My hands shook as I trimmed the wick. When the flame finally caught and the great lens began to turn, I let out a breath I had not known I was holding.

March 4 — No sleep. Every two hours I wound the clockwork that turns the lens, and every two hours I checked the oil. Near dawn, through the spray, I saw the lights of a schooner pass well clear of the rocks. I do not know her name. Her crew will never know mine. Still, I wept a little, and I am not ashamed to write it.

March 6 — The gale has blown itself out, and the doctor has come. Father is weak but awake. When Mother told him I had kept the light, he was quiet for a long time. Then he asked to see the logbook. He read every entry I had made—the times, the oil, the weather—and nodded.

“Neat hand,” he said. “Steady work.”

From Father, that is the highest praise there is. I think I will keep this diary, and I think I will keep the light, too, if they will let me.

passages.title: Counting Crabs: Citizen Scientists on the Delaware Bay
passages.text:
On calm nights in late May and June, when the moon is full or new, the beaches of the Delaware Bay fill with an ancient visitor. Horseshoe crabs, animals that have existed for more than 400 million years, crawl ashore by the thousands to lay their eggs in the sand.

For decades, scientists struggled to answer a simple question: how many horseshoe crabs are there? The bay's shoreline stretches for miles, and the spawning happens mostly at night. No single research team could watch every beach at once.

The solution came from ordinary people. Since 1990, volunteers have joined a yearly survey. Equipped with flashlights, clipboards, and a square frame called a quadrat, they walk set routes along the tide line. At regular intervals, they drop the quadrat and count every crab inside it. Scientists then use these samples to estimate the total population.

The data have revealed troubling trends. During the 1990s, crabs were harvested in large numbers for use as fishing bait. Counts dropped sharply. The decline mattered beyond the crabs themselves. Each spring, migrating shorebirds called red knots stop at the bay to feast on crab eggs before flying to the Arctic. With fewer eggs available, many red knots could not gain enough weight to complete their journey, and their numbers fell dramatically.

Citizen data helped persuade officials to act. New Jersey placed a moratorium on harvesting horseshoe crabs in 2008, and other states limited their harvests. Critics, including some people in the fishing industry, argued that the restrictions hurt their livelihoods and that the data were incomplete. Researchers responded that the volunteer survey, carried out with the same methods year after year, provided the most consistent record available.

The crab population has not fully recovered, and the debate continues. Still, the survey has shown what is possible when thousands of people with flashlights decide that a question is worth answering. As one longtime volunteer put it, "You don't need a degree to count. You just need to show up."

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a theme and analyze its development over the course of a text.
questions.question: Which theme is best developed in the story?
choices: Parents should not plan trips their children dislike.
Stepping away from familiar comforts can reveal unexpected strengths.
Maps are more reliable than phones in every situation.
Technology is always harmful to families.
questions.correctAnswer: Stepping away from familiar comforts can reveal unexpected strengths.
questions.explanation: Without his phone, Kenji uses his own knowledge to guide them, and his attitude changes.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how particular elements of a story interact (how setting shapes character).
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: How does the setting at the ridge contribute to a change in Kenji?
choices: The ridge has cell service, so he can look up directions.
The beautiful view makes him forget about his phone.
The rotted sign makes him angry at his father.
The approaching storm and broken sign create a real problem that pushes him to take part.
correctAnswers: The approaching storm and broken sign create a real problem that pushes him to take part.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence best shows the change described in Part A?
choices: They reached the car just as the first heavy drops began to fall.
“Which way?” Kenji asked, and for the first time his voice carried no sarcasm.
He held his phone above his head at every switchback.
correctAnswers: “Which way?” Kenji asked, and for the first time his voice carried no sarcasm.

questions.explanation: Facing the split trail and coming storm, Kenji drops the sarcasm and engages.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze the impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
questions.question: How does Kenji's line “Apparently I was listening” affect the tone of the scene?
choices: It adds light humor while showing he is surprised by his own knowledge.
It suggests that Kenji is lying to his father.
It shows that Kenji is angry at his teacher.
It makes the scene threatening and tense.
questions.correctAnswer: It adds light humor while showing he is surprised by his own knowledge.
questions.explanation: The dry remark is playful and self-aware.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite several pieces of textual evidence that most strongly support an inference.
questions.question: Select two details that suggest Kenji's attitude toward the trip has changed by the end.
choices: He glanced at the screen, then turned it face down on the seat.
“So,” he said, “where are we going next month?”
“It's called being cut off from civilization,” Kenji muttered.
He held his phone above his head at every switchback.
Dad pulled out a paper map and frowned.
correctAnswers: He glanced at the screen, then turned it face down on the seat.
“So,” he said, “where are we going next month?”
questions.explanation: Ignoring his phone and asking about the next trip show a new attitude.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how differences in characters' points of view create effects such as humor or suspense.
questions.question: How do the contrasting views of Dad and Kenji in paragraphs 2–3 affect the story?
choices: They establish a conflict about the trip that is resolved by the end.
They reveal that Dad is lost from the start.
They create suspense about the storm.
They show that Dad and Kenji agree about technology.
questions.correctAnswer: They establish a conflict about the trip that is resolved by the end.
questions.explanation: “Disconnecting” versus “cut off from civilization” sets up the attitude that later shifts.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a text's structure contributes to its meaning.
questions.question: Why does the author end the story with Kenji's question?
choices: to show his transformation through his own words rather than stating it directly
to show that Kenji is still bored
to set up a sequel about a new trip
to explain the science of topography
questions.correctAnswer: to show his transformation through his own words rather than stating it directly
questions.explanation: The question reveals that Kenji now wants to go hiking again.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a central idea and analyze its development.
questions.question: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: The question of later school start times involves both benefits and practical challenges that communities must weigh.
Bus routes are the only reason schools start early.
Later start times always reduce student attendance.
All middle schools should start at 8:30 a.m.
questions.correctAnswer: The question of later school start times involves both benefits and practical challenges that communities must weigh.
questions.explanation: The article presents both sides and concludes that the decision involves trade-offs.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Trace and evaluate an argument, assessing whether evidence is relevant and sufficient.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: Which piece of evidence most directly supports the argument for later start times?
choices: The recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics
The responsibility of caring for younger siblings
The concern that students will stay up later
The fact that buses serve several schools
correctAnswers: The recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which two additional details also support the argument for later start times? Select two.
choices: Later dismissal times may cut into after-school sports.
Researchers have reported improvements in attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class.
Some parents also worry that students will simply stay up later.
Changing bell schedules can affect bus routes.
During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night.
correctAnswers: During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night.
Researchers have reported improvements in attendance and fewer students falling asleep in class.

questions.explanation: Biology and research results support the case for later start times; the other details are counterarguments.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine an author's point of view and how the author acknowledges conflicting viewpoints.
questions.question: How does the author present the issue?
choices: by telling a personal story about being tired
by explaining arguments on both sides without taking a strong position
by arguing only for earlier start times
questions.correctAnswer: by explaining arguments on both sides without taking a strong position
questions.explanation: The author presents supporters, opponents, and compromises, then calls for careful weighing.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text.
questions.question: How does paragraph 4 contribute to the structure of the article?
choices: It summarizes the history of school buses.
It describes compromises that address concerns from both sides.
It introduces the debate for the first time.
It provides a definition of adolescence.
questions.correctAnswer: It describes compromises that address concerns from both sides.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains how districts balanced the issues.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including connotative meanings.
questions.question: In the last paragraph, what does trade-offs mean?
choices: giving up one benefit in order to gain another
questions.correctAnswer: giving up one benefit in order to gain another
questions.explanation: Each option has costs and benefits that must be balanced.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis.
questions.question: Select two concerns opponents raise about later start times.
choices: After-school activities and jobs may be affected.
Bus routes may need to change.
correctAnswers: Bus routes may need to change.
After-school activities and jobs may be affected.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists bus routes, after-school activities and responsibilities, and later bedtimes.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a theme and analyze its relationship to characters, setting, and plot.
questions.question: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: It is better to work quickly than carefully.
Apprentices should always disagree with their teachers.
Fishermen make better mapmakers than sailors.
True mastery requires understanding and checking information, not just copying it.
questions.correctAnswer: True mastery requires understanding and checking information, not just copying it.
questions.explanation: Tomas only earns the chance to make something new after he gathers real information himself.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a particular incident propels the action and reveals a character.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: How does the captain's visit affect Tomas?
choices: It proves that his copied map was perfect.
It shows him the danger of copying without verifying, which motivates him to investigate.
It convinces him to quit his apprenticeship.
It makes him angry at Master Ilse for blaming him.
correctAnswers: It shows him the danger of copying without verifying, which motivates him to investigate.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: Other apprentices in the city were already selling maps of their own.
She chose Tomas, a fisherman's son who could barely afford ink.
He copied coastlines, rivers, and the curling script of place names until his wrist ached.
The next morning, he borrowed his father's boat and spent a week sounding the harbor with a weighted rope.
correctAnswers: The next morning, he borrowed his father's boat and spent a week sounding the harbor with a weighted rope.

questions.explanation: Right after the captain's complaint, Tomas goes out to gather real depth data.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze the meaning and impact of specific word choices.
questions.question: What does the phrase “Tomas's face burned” reveal?
choices: He was excited about the captain's visit.
He felt ashamed of his mistake.
He was angry at the captain.
questions.correctAnswer: He felt ashamed of his mistake.
questions.explanation: A burning face suggests embarrassment after realizing he never checked the map.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how dialogue reveals aspects of a character.
questions.question: What does Ilse's answer, “When you understand why each line is where it is,” reveal about her?
choices: She believes copying is the only skill a mapmaker needs.
She values deep understanding over speed.
She is too busy to teach Tomas.
She does not want Tomas to succeed.
questions.correctAnswer: She values deep understanding over speed.
questions.explanation: She wants Tomas to understand the reasons behind the map before creating his own.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite textual evidence that most strongly supports an inference.
questions.question: Select two details that show Tomas becomes more thorough in his work.
choices: He spent a week sounding the harbor with a weighted rope, recording depths.
Tomas recognized the map as one he had copied.
He talked to fishermen, who knew the shifting sandbars better than any chart.
correctAnswers: He spent a week sounding the harbor with a weighted rope, recording depths.
He talked to fishermen, who knew the shifting sandbars better than any chart.
questions.explanation: Measuring depths and interviewing fishermen show careful research.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how structure contributes to meaning.
questions.question: How does the final line connect to an earlier part of the story?
choices: It answers Tomas's earlier question about when he will make something new.
It reveals the name of the port city.
questions.correctAnswer: It answers Tomas's earlier question about when he will make something new.
questions.explanation: Tomas asked “When will I make something new?” and Ilse finally says “Now, make something new.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine a central idea and analyze its development.
questions.question: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: The Wright brothers built bicycles before airplanes.
The Wright brothers' success came from learning from repeated failures through careful testing.
Kitty Hawk is the best place in the world to fly.
The first airplane flight lasted only twelve seconds.
questions.correctAnswer: The Wright brothers' success came from learning from repeated failures through careful testing.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes how failures and testing led to the 1903 flight.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze connections and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events.
questions.question: This question has two parts. Answer Part A, then answer Part B.

parts.label: Part A
parts.question: Part A: What led the Wright brothers to build a wind tunnel?
choices: They wanted to sell wind tunnels to other inventors.
They suspected the published data they used was inaccurate.
They needed a place to store their gliders.
correctAnswers: They suspected the published data they used was inaccurate.

parts.label: Part B
parts.question: Part B: Which sentence best supports the answer to Part A?
choices: The flight covered only about 120 feet.
Beginning in 1899, Wilbur and Orville Wright built and tested a series of kites and gliders.
They suspected that the published measurements they had relied on were wrong.
correctAnswers: They suspected that the published measurements they had relied on were wrong.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that doubts about the old data led to the wind tunnel experiments.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how the author distinguishes it from others.
questions.question: How does the author's view of the first flight differ from the way it is “often described”?
choices: The author believes the flight never happened.
The author thinks the flight was unimportant.
The author sees it as the result of years of work, not a sudden triumph.
The author argues that Wilbur flew the plane, not Orville.
questions.correctAnswer: The author sees it as the result of years of work, not a sudden triumph.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 contrasts the popular idea of sudden success with the reality of years of failure.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Determine the meaning of technical words in context.
questions.question: Based on paragraph 4, what is the purpose of “wing warping”?
choices: to help the pilot balance and turn the aircraft
to measure the lift of curved wings
questions.correctAnswer: to help the pilot balance and turn the aircraft
questions.explanation: The passage says wing warping twisted the wings to help the pilot balance and turn.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite textual evidence.
questions.question: Select two details that show the brothers' persistence.

The flight was shorter than a jumbo jet's wingspan.
They tested more than 200 wing shapes.
After the poor 1901 glider, they questioned their data instead of quitting.
Orville lay on the lower wing of the aircraft.
correctAnswers: They tested more than 200 wing shapes.
After the poor 1901 glider, they questioned their data instead of quitting.
questions.explanation: Both details show the brothers kept working through setbacks.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a key sentence develops and refines an idea.

choices: to emphasize how short the flight was despite its importance
to argue that modern jets are unsafe
to explain how jumbo jets were invented
to show that the Wright plane was larger than a jet
questions.correctAnswer: to emphasize how short the flight was despite its importance
questions.explanation: The comparison highlights the small distance of a world-changing event.

questions.skill: Determine a theme and analyze its development.

choices: Taking on responsibility in a crisis can reveal courage and purpose.
Doctors should live closer to lighthouses.
Storms are more powerful than people.
Lighthouse work is too dangerous for young people.
questions.correctAnswer: Taking on responsibility in a crisis can reveal courage and purpose.
questions.explanation: The narrator steps up to keep the light and discovers she wants to continue doing it.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a character develops over the course of a text.

choices: She stays equally nervous from beginning to end.
She moves from confidence to fear of the lighthouse.
She moves from anger at her father to forgiveness.
She moves from uncertainty about the job to confidence that she wants to keep doing it.
correctAnswers: She moves from uncertainty about the job to confidence that she wants to keep doing it.

parts.question: Part B: Which two quotations best support the answer to Part A? Select two.
choices: The doctor from the mainland cannot cross until the gale passes.

I think I will keep this diary, and I think I will keep the light, too, if they will let me.
He read every entry I had made—the times, the oil, the weather—and nodded.
correctAnswers: My hands shook as I trimmed the wick.
I think I will keep this diary, and I think I will keep the light, too, if they will let me.

questions.explanation: Her shaking hands show early uncertainty, and her final wish shows new confidence.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze the impact of word choice on meaning and tone.

Seeing someone perform a task is different from being responsible for it yourself.
She could not see the lamp from the house.
She was not allowed to watch her father work.
questions.correctAnswer: Seeing someone perform a task is different from being responsible for it yourself.
questions.explanation: She realizes that observing her father didn't fully prepare her.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Analyze how a text's form (diary) contributes to its meaning.

choices: It reveals the narrator's private thoughts and feelings as events unfold.
It hides the narrator's emotions from the reader.
It provides an objective news report of the storm.
It allows the reader to know what every character is thinking.
questions.correctAnswer: It reveals the narrator's private thoughts and feelings as events unfold.
questions.explanation: Dated first-person entries show her personal reactions, such as weeping when the schooner passes.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Cite evidence to support an inference about a character.

From Father, that is the highest praise there is.

questions.explanation: His brief words are described as his highest praise.

Horseshoe crabs are the oldest animals on Earth.
Red knots are the most important birds on the Delaware Bay.

Red knots began to eat fishing bait instead of eggs.

The crab population has not fully recovered, and the debate continues.
correctAnswers: With fewer eggs available, many red knots could not gain enough weight to complete their journey, and their numbers fell dramatically.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 links fewer crab eggs to red knots being unable to gain weight for migration.

questions.subject: ela

a reward for catching more crabs

questions.explanation: A gerund is a verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun (here, the subject).

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Form and use verbs in the conditional and subjunctive mood.
questions.question:
Which word correctly completes the sentence?

If I ___ the principal, I would add more time for recess.
questions.explanation: The subjunctive mood uses “were” for hypothetical situations.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use an ellipsis to indicate an omission.
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses an ellipsis to show that words were left out of a quotation?
choices: The speech said … “We will build a stronger community.”
The speech said, “We will build a stronger community” …
The speech said, “We will build … a stronger community …”…
The speech said, “We will build a stronger … community.”
questions.correctAnswer: The speech said, “We will build a stronger … community.”
questions.explanation: An ellipsis inside the quotation marks shows where words were omitted.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use a comma, ellipsis, or dash to indicate a pause or break.
questions.question: Which sentence uses a dash correctly?
choices: We packed—everything we needed tents, food, and flashlights.
We—packed everything we needed, tents, food, and flashlights.
We packed everything we needed—tents, food, and flashlights.
We packed everything we—needed tents, food, and flashlights.
questions.correctAnswer: We packed everything we needed—tents, food, and flashlights.
questions.explanation: A dash can introduce a list that explains what came before it.

questions.explanation: “Affect” is usually a verb meaning “to influence.”

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Use verbs in the active and passive voice to achieve particular effects.
questions.question: A writer wants to emphasize the mural rather than who painted it. Which sentence does this best?
choices: Students completed the mural last spring.
The students worked hard last spring.
The mural was completed last spring.
questions.correctAnswer: The mural was completed last spring.
questions.explanation: Passive voice puts the focus on the receiver of the action, the mural.

questions.question: Which word has the most positive connotation to describe someone who saves money carefully?
questions.explanation: “Thrifty” suggests wise saving; the other words suggest an unwillingness to share.

questions.subject: ela
questions.skill: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., verbal irony, puns) in context.
questions.question: Which sentence is an example of verbal irony?
choices: Stepping into the freezing rain, Jaden said, “What lovely weather for a picnic.”
Jaden ran inside to escape the rain.
The rain fell like tiny needles.
Jaden said the rain was cold.
questions.correctAnswer: Stepping into the freezing rain, Jaden said, “What lovely weather for a picnic.”
questions.explanation: Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what you mean.
